title: Hook sizes explained
subtitle: What the hook size numbers mean, how they relate to yarn weight, and when to deviate
excerpt: Hook sizes are measured in millimetres. The larger the number, the wider the hook and the bigger the stitch. Yarn weight and pattern gauge guide the starting size; your tension swatch tells you whether to go up or down.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The diameter of the hook shaft in millimetres. This is the measurement that determines stitch size; a larger hook produces larger stitches with the same yarn.
The number of stitches and rows that fit in a measured area, usually 10 cm. Used to confirm the finished piece will come out the right size.

content.text: The
hook size
is the diameter of the hook shaft in millimetres. It is the main tool for controlling
gauge

: a larger hook makes bigger stitches; a smaller hook makes smaller ones. UK, European, and US hook brands all use millimetres as the primary measurement, though older US hooks use a letter system (B, C, D...) alongside the mm size.
Common hook sizes and their yarn weight range
2.0 to 3.5 mm: lace weight and 4-ply (fingering). Used for fine shawls, socks, and doilies.
3.5 to 4.5 mm: DK weight. Most common range for garments, toys, and lightweight blankets.
4.5 to 6.0 mm: aran weight. Sweaters, accessories, medium blankets.
6.0 to 9.0 mm: chunky weight. Quick projects, cushions, heavy scarves.
10 mm and above: super bulky and jumbo. Chunky blankets and baskets, usually with multiple strands held together.
Ball band recommendation versus pattern recommendation

The ball band lists a suggested hook size for average gauge. The pattern also lists a hook size. These may differ slightly. The pattern's gauge is what you are aiming for; the ball band size is a starting point. Always work a gauge swatch and adjust if needed, regardless of what both say.
When to deviate from the recommended size
Your swatch is smaller than gauge: go up one hook size.
Your swatch is larger than gauge: go down one hook size.
Foundation chain is too tight: work the chain one hook size up, then switch back to the project hook.
Amigurumi: work one hook size smaller than the ball band to close the fabric so stuffing does not show through.
Common problems

items.symptom: Two hooks labelled the same size produce slightly different gauges
items.cause: Manufacturing tolerances vary between brands. A 4.0 mm from one brand can be fractionally different from a 4.0 mm from another.
items.fix: Use the same hook brand throughout a project. If changing hook brand mid-project, work a gauge swatch with the new hook first.

items.symptom: The hook size on the pattern does not match any hook in the collection
items.cause: The pattern uses an intermediate size (such as 3.75 mm) that not all sets include.
items.fix: Use the nearest size available and check gauge. A 3.75 mm pattern can often be worked on a 4.0 mm or 3.5 mm with a small tension adjustment.

content.text: What to try next

Work a gauge swatch for the project you are about to start using the pattern's stated hook size. Compare to the stated gauge before making any hook changes. See the tension adjustment guide if the swatch needs correcting.
